title: Austin Scholar #232: The Neuroscience Behind Why Alpha Works
author: Austin Scholar
summary: A Stanford student who writes about learning science reviews a Huberman Lab podcast episode featuring Alpha School principal Joe Liemandt, and uses cognitive load theory to resolve what initially sounds like a contradiction between the two speakers about whether learning requires struggle. Huberman argues learning is driven entirely by an 'error signal' -- a mismatch between what a learner expected and what actually happened -- meaning a student who gets every problem right has no signal prompting the brain to change, while Liemandt argues 'suffering isn't the best way to learn' and that Alpha's fast method is a worked example with progressively-removed scaffolding rather than pure unscaffolded struggle. The author's resolution is that John Sweller's 1988 distinction between germane load (the productive effort of building a new idea, which does generate the error signal Huberman describes) and extraneous load (everything else competing for working memory -- confusing instructions, a noisy room, having to manually compute 7x8 mid-problem -- which produces identical-feeling frustration but zero neuroplasticity) shows the two speakers aren't actually disagreeing: Alpha's worked-example method strips out extraneous load so that only germane, productive struggle remains. The piece also relays Liemandt's 'working memory slots' framing (a student stuck at a 710 math SAT score improved to 790 simply by memorizing multiplication tables, freeing up slots for algebra) and a 2017 study finding cognitive capacity drops merely from having one's own phone face-down on the desk nearby, interpreted by Huberman as evidence the brain computes the phone's presence unconsciously even without active checking.
points: The essay's central intellectual contribution is resolving an apparent contradiction between Huberman ('without struggle, there's no learning') and Liemandt ('suffering isn't the best way to learn') using Sweller's germane-versus-extraneous load distinction: both kinds of difficulty feel identical from the inside, but only germane load (building the actual new idea) generates the error signal that drives neuroplasticity.

The multiplication-tables anecdote (a student's math SAT score jumping from 710 to 790 purely from memorizing times tables) operationalizes 'working memory slots' as a concrete, measurable mechanism: automating a low-level computation frees the capacity needed for higher-level algebraic reasoning.

The 2017 phone study -- cognitive capacity dropping merely from a phone being face-down nearby, recovering only once it left the room -- is used as evidence that the brain computes a phone's presence unconsciously, reframing 'distraction' as an involuntary cognitive-load tax rather than a simple willpower or focus failure.

Worked examples with progressively-faded scaffolding are presented as the practical resolution to the struggle-versus-scaffolding debate: they strip away extraneous load (confusing instructions, unclear steps) so that the only difficulty remaining is the genuinely productive kind, ensuring students receive real error signals without wasted, unproductive frustration.
quotes: Liemandt told the story of a student who'd stalled at a 710 on the math SAT, went back and memorized her multiplication tables, and came back with a 790. "She was just running out of working memory slots.
His read on it: "It's not really a focus issue. It's that the brain is computing consciously and unconsciously.

If a brain or a body can execute a particular thing... there is no reason for it to change... the error signal is what actually drives the opportunity for change. And so, without errors, there's no struggle, and therefore, without struggle, there's no learning.

Then about forty minutes later, Liemandt says that "maybe suffering isn't the best way to learn for most people. If I can teach you something and it doesn't require suffering, that's better than requiring suffering." And when Huberman asks how Alpha actually teaches, Liemandt is emphatic that "here's a math problem, figure it out" is the slow way.

John Sweller, who developed cognitive load theory in a 1988 paper in Cognitive Science, called this germane load. The error signal Huberman talks about shows here. The second kind is everything else competing for those same working memory slots: confusing instructions, a noisy room, a phone in the backpack, having to compute 7x8 mid-problem.

Those worked examples with fading scaffolds that Liemandt talked about strip away the extraneous load so the only hard thing left is the new material itself. This method clears out the junk struggle so that the good kind can happen -- so that you can be sure that your kid is receiving the right error signals.
